title: Electrochemical Reduction of Nitrobenzene via Redox-Mediated Chronoamperometry
author: Stergiou, Broadhurst, et al.
materials:
Timing: 1 h
5.A two-compartment H-cell equipped with a proton-exchange membrane will be required for the electro-reduction process. In this case, a custom-made two-compartment cell (see Figure 1) was used to perform the reduction of nitrobenzene. Each side has a 35 mL capacity. A circular sealing ring is placed between the two compartments.a.The cell must be cleaned thoroughly with deionized water and acetone and dried completely before starting.b.Construct the cell so that it is leak-free. To ensure that there is no leakage in this example, Teflon tape is wrapped around the male-end threading of each compartment joint (see Figure 2).Figure 2Teflon tape used at the threading of the compartment joint to prevent leakagec.Insert the sealing ring and then join the male ends together with the threaded H-cell connector (item D in Figure 3).Figure 3Overall diagram of the components of the electrochemical reaction, with parts labeled as follows(A) Working side of the H-cell.(B) Counter side of the H-cell.(C) Sealing ring with Nafion membrane.(D) H-cell connector.(E) Teflon tape.(F) BioLogic SP-150 potentiostat.(G) Syringe needle for N2 purge.(H) Ag/AgCl reference electrode.(I) Working and counter electrodes.(J) Stirring bar.d.Test the cell by filling each compartment with deionized water and check for any leaks over a period of about 30 min prior to use (see troubleshooting 1). steps.title: Assemble H‑cell
steps.instruction: Clean a custom two‑compartment H‑cell (35 mL per compartment) with deionized water and acetone, dry completely, wrap Teflon tape around each male‑end thread, insert the sealing ring with Nafion membrane, join the compartments with the threaded connector, and test for leaks by filling both sides with deionized water for ~30 min before emptying.

substeps.instruction: Clean cell with deionized water and acetone; dry thoroughly.
Wrap Teflon tape around each male‑end threading of the compartment joints.
Insert sealing ring and join male ends with the H‑cell connector.
Fill each compartment with deionized water, check for leaks for ~30 min, then empty.

steps.title: Prepare electrodes
steps.instruction: Cut two rectangles of carbon felt (1.8 × 2 cm, geometric area) for working and counter electrodes (counter electrode may be equal or larger), attach stainless‑steel crocodile clips, and keep the Ag/AgCl reference electrode (3 M NaCl) in a 3 M NaCl storage solution when not in use.

substeps.instruction: Cut two carbon‑felt rectangles 1.8 × 2 cm.
Connect each electrode to the potentiostat with stainless‑steel crocodile clips.
Store Ag/AgCl reference electrode in 3 M NaCl solution when idle.

steps.title: Prepare electrolyte solutions
steps.instruction: Prepare the electrolyte solutions containing phosphotungstic acid as described in the supporting information (if needed).

steps.title: Extract aniline into chloroform
steps.instruction: Transfer the working‑cell (WC) contents to a 250 mL separating funnel, rinse the WC flask with deionized water then chloroform adding each wash to the funnel; transfer the opposite‑side (OP) flask contents to the same funnel, rinse the OP flask three times with chloroform adding each wash, then perform three 50 mL chloroform extractions, collecting the organic phases in the OP flask; keep the aqueous phase in a clean conical flask for later analysis.

substeps.instruction: Transfer WC flask contents to separating funnel; rinse WC flask with deionized water and add washings to funnel.
Rinse WC flask with chloroform and add washings to funnel.
Transfer OP flask contents to same funnel; rinse OP flask three times with chloroform, adding each wash.
Perform three extractions with ~50 mL chloroform each; collect organic phases in OP flask.
Collect the remaining aqueous phase in a clean conical flask for later use.

steps.title: Wash organic extracts
steps.instruction: Place the combined organic extracts back into a clean separating funnel and wash three times with 20 mL deionized water each; drain the washed organic layer into a clean conical flask and set the aqueous washes aside.

substeps.instruction: Return combined organic extracts to a clean separating funnel.
Wash three times with 20 mL deionized water per wash.
Drain the washed organic layer into a clean conical flask.
Keep the aqueous washings aside for later analysis.

steps.title: Dry organic extract
steps.instruction: Add magnesium sulfate slowly to the organic extract while gyrating until excess magnesium sulfate flows freely, then filter the mixture under gravity using a funnel with filter paper; wash the filter cake with small portions of chloroform and collect the filtrate.

substeps.instruction: Add magnesium sulfate slowly while gyrating until free‑flowing.
Set up a clean conical flask, funnel, and filter paper.
Pour the mixture through the funnel; filter under gravity.
Wash the filter paper with small amounts of chloroform and combine washes with filtrate.

steps.title: Concentrate organic phase
steps.instruction: Weigh a clean 250 mL or 500 mL round‑bottom flask, transfer the filtered chloroform solution (and rinses) into it, and evaporate on a rotary evaporator set to 45 °C water bath and 450 mbar pressure, slowly reducing pressure to avoid rapid suction; after complete removal of chloroform, apply high vacuum for ≥30 min, cool to 20‑25 °C, and re‑weigh to record gross yield.

substeps.instruction: Weigh clean 250 mL or 500 mL round‑bottom flask.
Transfer filtered chloroform solution and rinses into flask.
Rotary evaporate at 45 °C water bath, 450 mbar pressure; reduce pressure slowly.
After solvent removal, apply high vacuum for at least 30 min.
Cool flask to 20‑25 °C and re‑weigh to note gross yield.

steps.title: Prepare NMR sample
steps.instruction: Dissolve the residue from the round‑bottom flask in 0.5 mL deuterated chloroform, transfer the solution with a syringe or pipette into a labeled NMR tube, and acquire a ^1H NMR spectrum (note that N‑phenylhydroxylamine and azoxybenzene may appear as side‑product peaks).

substeps.instruction: Redissolve residue in 0.5 mL CDCl₃.
Transfer solution to a labeled NMR tube using syringe or pipette.
Record the ^1H NMR spectrum.

steps.title: Analyze NMR data
steps.instruction: Identify and assign peaks for the desired aniline product and any other species, integrate all peaks, compare integrals of product versus starting material to calculate conversion, compare product integrals to total integrals to calculate selectivity, and combine gross yield, conversion, and selectivity to obtain isolated yield.

substeps.instruction: Identify/assign expected product peaks and any other peaks.
Integrate all peaks.
Calculate conversion by comparing product and starting‑material integrals (using equivalent proton counts).
Calculate selectivity by comparing product integrals to the sum of all product‑related integrals.
Use gross yield, conversion, and selectivity to compute isolated yield.

steps.title: Calculate chronoamperometric metrics
steps.instruction: From the potentiostat software, use the current recorded over the first ~2.5 h to compute average current density (mA cm⁻²) by dividing by the working electrode geometric area; then calculate Faradaic efficiency using the total charge passed, the isolated product mass, n = 6 electrons per nitrobenzene, and Faraday’s constant (96 485 C mol⁻¹) via the provided equations.

substeps.instruction: Average current density = (average current over ~2.5 h) ÷ (geometric area of working electrode).
Calculate theoretical moles of product from charge (Q) using Q = m · n · F (n = 6).
Determine actual moles from isolated mass.
Faradaic efficiency (%) = (actual moles / theoretical moles) × 100.

description: Aromatic amines (anilines) are essential building blocks, extensively used in the industrial sector for the synthesis of pharmaceuticals, plastics, dyes, and agrochemicals (Kadam and Tilve, 2015; Jurado-Sanchez et al., 2013). A typical example of such a compound is the substituted nitrobenzene p-aminophenol, which is used as a precursor in the synthesis of one of the most widely produced pharmaceuticals, paracetamol (Ellis, 2002). At present, the most widespread route for the synthesis of these compounds is through the reduction of their corresponding nitrobenzenes (Travis, 2009). However, these transformations require the use of high temperatures (about 300°C) and pressures (5 bar), the use of extremely flammable hydrogen gas as well as expensive metal-based catalysts (Pt, Ni, Pd, or Cu) (Formenti et al., 2019). These routes are usually very effective for the reduction of the simple un-substituted nitrobenzene but their selectivity for the production of functionalized nitroarenes is somewhat more variable (Formenti et al., 2019). A prime example of such suboptimal selectivity is the transformation of o-nitroiodobenzene to its corresponding aniline derivative, where the halogen is readily cleaved from the benzene ring causing the formation of side products (Pietrowski, 2012; Baumeister et al., 1991). To tackle the selectivity issue in the reduction of substituted nitrobenzenes, more recent approaches have focused on the use of a different hydrogenation agent (other than H2) and less harsh reaction conditions (Gladiali and Alberico, 2006; Samec et al., 2006). One alternative is the use of dissolved hydrogenation agents such as hydrazine and formate in the presence of metal catalysts (Layek et al., 2012; Doherty et al., 2019; Garcia-Verdugo et al., 2006). The use of these reagents, however, raises some questions concerning sustainability as these compounds are toxic and are irreversibly consumed during the hydrogenation process.
